title: JPA transactions, lazy loading & N+1
summary: @Transactional boundaries and proxies, rollback rules for checked exceptions, LazyInitializationException and open-in-view, default fetch types, the N+1 problem and its fixes (JOIN FETCH, entity graphs, batch fetching, DTO projections), and optimistic locking.
lesson:
## @Transactional

```java
@Service
public class CheckoutService {
    @Transactional
    public Order checkout(long cartId) { ... }          // one transaction: all or nothing

    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    public OrderView view(long id) { ... }              // hints the flush mode and the driver
}
```

- The annotation works through a **proxy**: only calls that come from another bean start the transaction. `this.checkout(...)` from inside the same class bypasses it (self-invocation).
- Default propagation is `REQUIRED`: join an existing transaction or start one.
- **Rollback rules**: by default only unchecked exceptions (`RuntimeException`) and `Error`s roll back. A **checked** exception thrown out of the method COMMITS the transaction unless you declare `@Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class)`.
- Put transactions on service methods (a business operation), not on controllers or repositories one by one.

## Lazy loading and LazyInitializationException

Default fetch types: `@ManyToOne` and `@OneToOne` are **EAGER**, `@OneToMany` and `@ManyToMany` are **LAZY**. Mark `@ManyToOne` lazy explicitly (`fetch = FetchType.LAZY`) to avoid loading half the database.

A lazy association is a proxy that queries when first touched. Touching it after the persistence context closed throws `LazyInitializationException: could not initialize proxy - no Session`. Classic triggers: serialising an entity to JSON in a controller after the service transaction ended, or accessing `order.getLines()` in a background thread.

Spring Boot enables **open-in-view** by default (and logs a warning about it): the persistence context stays open until the response is written, which hides LazyInitializationException but runs lazy queries during view rendering, outside your transaction, often as N+1. Many teams set `spring.jpa.open-in-view=false` and load what each use case needs explicitly.

## The N+1 problem

```java
List<Order> orders = repo.findAll();                // 1 query
for (Order o : orders) o.getCustomer().getName();   // + 1 query per order (lazy customer)
```

Fixes:
- **JOIN FETCH**: `@Query("select o from Order o join fetch o.customer")` loads both in one query.
- **Entity graphs**: `@EntityGraph(attributePaths = "customer") List<Order> findByStatus(String s);`
- **Batch fetching**: `@BatchSize(size = 100)` or `hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size` loads lazy associations for many parents with `WHERE id IN (...)` queries: N+1 becomes 1 + N/100.
- **DTO projections**: `select new com.x.OrderRow(o.id, c.name) from Order o join o.customer c`, ideal for read endpoints.

Caveat: `join fetch` of a COLLECTION combined with pagination makes Hibernate apply the limit in memory (it warns: HHH90003004). Page the parent ids first, then fetch their children.

## Optimistic locking

A `@Version` field is checked and incremented on every update; if another transaction updated the row first, the save fails with an optimistic locking exception (`ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException` in Spring), which an API maps to **409 Conflict**.

## Checklist for a read endpoint

`@Transactional(readOnly = true)` service method, an explicit fetch plan (join fetch, entity graph or a DTO projection), a page size cap, and the generated SQL checked once in the logs (`spring.jpa.show-sql` or `logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=debug`).

quiz.prompt: A `@Transactional` method throws a CHECKED exception (no rollbackFor). What happens to the transaction?
choices: It rolls back, as it would for any exception
It commits the changes made before the throw
It stays open until the caller handles it
It is retried once before rolling back
quiz.explanation: Only RuntimeException and Error roll back by default; add rollbackFor for checked exceptions.

quiz.prompt: Method `a()` in a bean calls `this.b()`, where only `b()` is `@Transactional`. Is a transaction started for b?
choices: Yes: the annotation is honoured on any call to b()
No: a transaction needs @Transactional on the class
Yes: Spring weaves the annotation into the bytecode
No: the self-call bypasses the transactional proxy
quiz.explanation: Move b to another bean or annotate the entry point.

quiz.prompt: What is the default fetch type of `@ManyToOne`?
choices: `EAGER`
`LAZY`
`BATCH`
`NONE`
quiz.explanation: ToOne associations are eager by default; collections are lazy.

choices: When an entity is persisted before its id has been generated
When two transactions update the same row at once
When a lazy association is read after the session closes
When a query for a single entity returns no rows
quiz.explanation: Load what you need inside the transaction or map to DTOs there.

quiz.prompt: Listing 200 orders and reading each order's lazy customer issues how many queries?
quiz.explanation: One for the orders plus one per order: the N+1 problem.

quiz.prompt: Which fixes the N+1 for order customers in ONE query?
choices: `select o from Order o join fetch o.customer`
`select o from Order o join o.customer`
`@ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)`
`select o from Order o where o.customer is not null`
quiz.explanation: join fetch loads the association together with the orders.

quiz.prompt: What does `@BatchSize(size = 100)` on a lazy association change?
choices: Nothing, unless the association is also declared EAGER
It switches the association to eager fetching
It caps the association at 100 loaded child rows
Lazy loads are grouped into IN queries of up to 100 ids

quiz.prompt: What is a known risk of Spring Boot's default open-in-view?
choices: It keeps one transaction open for the whole request
It disables lazy loading on every entity association
Lazy loads fire during rendering, hiding N+1 queries
It forbids @Transactional on methods in web controllers
quiz.explanation: Many teams disable it and fetch explicitly per use case. Those lazy loads run outside the service's transaction.

quiz.prompt: Two users update the same order; it has a `@Version` field. The second commit...
choices: fails with an optimistic locking exception
overwrites the first commit without any error
merges both changes into one row version
waits for a row lock held by the first user
quiz.explanation: The version check detects the concurrent update. The exception is usually mapped to 409 Conflict.

quiz.prompt: Why is `join fetch` of a collection plus pagination problematic?
choices: JPQL rejects join fetch combined with setMaxResults
Hibernate applies the limit in memory after loading all rows
The fetched collections arrive empty when paged
Spring Data cannot page queries that use join fetch
quiz.explanation: Page the parent ids first, then fetch the children for that page.

flashcards.back: Unchecked exceptions and errors roll back; checked exceptions commit unless rollbackFor includes them.
It is applied by a proxy, so a method invoked through this from the same bean runs without it.
ManyToOne and OneToOne are eager; OneToMany and ManyToMany are lazy.
Touching a lazy association after its persistence context has closed, for example while serialising outside the transaction.

flashcards.front: Four fixes for N+1 in JPA
flashcards.back: join fetch, an entity graph, batch fetching with IN queries, or a DTO projection query.
Keeping the persistence context open until the response is written; it hides lazy-loading errors but runs queries outside your transaction.
Hibernate warns and paginates in memory; page the parents first, then fetch their children.
Each update checks and bumps the version; a stale update fails and should become a 409 response.

drills.title: Turn N+1 into batched IN queries
drills.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "The order export loads each order's customer lazily: 50,000 orders, 50,001 queries. The database allows at most 500 ids per IN list. Load customers in batches."

**Why it matters.** Batch fetching (what `@BatchSize` and `hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size` do) collects the ids you will need and loads them with a few `WHERE id IN (...)` queries, respecting the database's IN-list limit.

**Your task.** Implement `static List<OrderRow> withCustomers(List<Order> orders, Function<Set<Long>, Map<Long, Customer>> loadCustomers, int batchSize)`:
- collect the DISTINCT customer ids of the orders, in first-seen order
- call `loadCustomers` with batches of at most `batchSize` ids each, every id in exactly one batch (so the number of calls is the distinct count divided by the batch size, rounded up)
- return one `OrderRow(orderId, customerName)` per order, in the orders' order; a customer missing from every result gives the name `"(unknown)"`
- no orders: no calls and an empty list; `batchSize` below 1 throws `IllegalArgumentException`

**Worked example.** 5 orders for customers 1, 2, 3, 1, 4 with batch size 2 cause 2 calls ({1, 2} and {3, 4}).
hints: First work out the set of ids you will need, then split that set into chunks no bigger than the limit.
Collect distinct customer ids with a LinkedHashSet, loop i from 0 by batchSize taking subList windows, putAll each loader result into one map, then map every order to a row with a fallback name.

Gather each customer id once in the order first seen, fetch them in windows of at most the allowed size, combine all the answers into one lookup, and build a row for every order, using the placeholder when a customer was not returned.
